deterministic_subtrack.expert_lesson: Any field-programmable non-volatile memory — one-time-programmable, fuse-based, multiple-time-programmable, antifuse — separates two operations with different electrical needs. READING needs only the core supply. PROGRAMMING needs a SEPARATE supply that is sourced from OUTSIDE the die, sits ABOVE the core voltage, and enters through a dedicated terminal. Nothing on-die produces a voltage above the core rail, so the programming supply can never come from the internal power grid; it has to arrive on a package pin or a wafer-probe pad. Treat this as a property of the storage mechanism rather than a vendor option: two unrelated programmable-memory IP families characterised on one process — one process-native, one third-party — specify it identically, both externally supplied and both above the core rail. So when an input instantiates such a memory AND describes programming control (a program request, an address, data, a busy/done handshake), the design is stating it intends to burn the array: ask where the programming supply enters, and capture it as a first-class terminal in the pin/pad table and as its own rail in the power-intent layer, kept distinct from the core rail. Capture the read path too — it needs the core supply alone, so a design that only reads a pre-programmed array legitimately has no such terminal, and the two cases must not be conflated. Nothing in a digital flow observes this gap: simulation, elaboration, synthesis, timing, DRC and LVS are all clean because the logic is entirely well-formed. It first appears at bring-up, on silicon, as an array that will not accept a burn.
